content: Bacterial vaginosis (BV) is a prevalent cause of vaginitis and is associated with significant obstetric and gynecologic complications, as well as an increased risk of HIV-1 transmission. This has prompted renewed interest in its treatment. The objective of this study was to evaluate the efficacy of antimicrobial agents in treating BV in non-pregnant women. The researchers conducted a comprehensive search of multiple databases, including the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL), MEDLINE, EMBASE, LILACS, and African Healthline, up to December 2007. They also reviewed proceedings from relevant international conferences dating back to 1981. The study included randomized controlled trials that compared two or more antimicrobial agents, or antimicrobial agents versus placebo or no treatment, in women diagnosed with BV based on clinical or Gram-stain criteria. Two authors independently assessed the quality of the trials and extracted data, which was then cross-checked by a third author. A total of 24 trials involving 4,422 participants were reviewed. Most of these trials focused on symptomatic women. Only seven trials analyzed results using an intention-to-treat approach, and the remaining trials were re-analyzed by the researchers. Clindamycin demonstrated a significantly lower rate of treatment failure compared to placebo, with a relative risk (RR) of 0.25 (95% confidence interval [CI] 0.16 to 0.37). When comparing clindamycin and metronidazole, the rates of treatment failure were similar, regardless of the regimen type, at both two-week and four-week follow-ups (RR 1.01, 95% CI 0.69 to 1.46; RR 0.91, 95% CI 0.70 to 1.18, respectively). Clindamycin was associated with fewer adverse events compared to metronidazole (RR 0.75, 95% CI 0.56 to 1.02). However, metronidazole was more likely to cause a metallic taste (RR 0.08, 95% CI 0.01 to 0.59) and nausea or vomiting (RR 0.23, 95% CI 0.10 to 0.51). Lactobacillus, when administered intravaginally as gelatin tablets, was more effective than oral metronidazole (RR 0.20, 95% CI 0.05 to 0.08). Additionally, a combination of oral lactobacillus and metronidazole was more effective than metronidazole alone (RR 0.33, 95% CI 0.14 to 0.77). Clindamycin showed a lower rate of clinical failure compared to triple sulfonamide cream (RR 0.46, 95% CI 0.29 to 0.72). In contrast, hydrogen peroxide douche was associated with a higher rate of clinical failure (RR 1.75, 95% CI 1.02 to 3.00) and more adverse events (RR 2.33, 95% CI 1.21 to 4.52) compared to a single 2 g dose of metronidazole. In conclusion, clindamycin preparations, oral metronidazole, and both oral and intravaginal lactobacillus tablets were effective treatments for BV. However, hydrogen peroxide douche and triple sulfonamide cream were found to be ineffective. Metronidazole was associated with side effects such as metallic taste, nausea, and vomiting. The authors emphasized the need for better-designed trials with larger sample sizes to further evaluate the efficacy of promising treatments.
